transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Aisha Rahman (CTO, Sprigwell), Tom Ellis (Head of Eng), Maya Chen (Data Lead)

Summary (auto): Quick model catalog walkthrough focusing on open models, benchmark tradeoffs, and compatibility matrix for a private/dedicated pilot. Customer concerned about latency SLOs, data residency, and on-prem GPU compatibility. Next steps: share slides, benchmarks, compatibility matrix, and schedule infra deep-dive.

Topics: model catalog overview, benchmarks (p50/p95/p99), quantization & compatibility, hosted vs dedicated vs private, integration points (API/Console/Optimize), security (SOC2/SAML/KMS), pilot pricing and SLAs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 45 minutes, we'll run through the model catalog and then leave time for q's. Marco will jump into the benchmark bits and compatibility matrix.
[00:18] Dr. Aisha: Great thanks Lena, excited. Quick context: we're a mid-size clinic network, most traffic is conversational triage and some summarization. We care a lot about p99 under 200ms for short consult flows.
[00:33] Tom Ellis: And we have on-prem GPU nodes for PHI workloads, plus a VPC setup in our cloud for less sensitive calls.
[00:44] Marco Ruiz: Awesome, that helps. I'll try to keep the technical bits concrete — sequence lengths, batching behavior, quant profiles.
[01:02] Lena Park: Okay first slide, model catalog. We curate open models and profile them for inference — latency, throughput, cost per token, and compatibility. We expose variants: fp16, int8 quant, and some 4-bit quant profiles that we call q4-fast / q4-precise in the catalog.
[01:30] Maya Chen: Quick question, are the q4 names standard? We have internal folks who ask about quant profile stability.
[01:38] Marco Ruiz: Yeah, nomenclature is Redwood-internal — sorry sometimes the export shows "Redwood Optima" or similar, transcription typo — but q4-fast vs q4-precise map to different quantization tradeoffs. q4-fast favors speed and smaller memory, q4-precise favors quality.
[02:02] Dr. Aisha: Do you have benchmarks for these on on-prem A100s?
[02:08] Marco Ruiz: We do. I'll show a table. Important caveat: our numbers are sequence-length and batch-dependent. For a 32-token request single-stream on A100s, you might see p50 ~40ms, p95 ~120ms, p99 ~200-240ms for a medium-sized Llama-variant in q4-fast. In fp16 it's faster for quality but memory heavy; int8 is middle ground.
[02:35] Tom Ellis: Are those numbers for a single request or with batching turned on?
[02:39] Marco Ruiz: Single-stream, no batching. With batching (continuous batching) we can get much better throughput but p99 increases with queueing. Our Optimize tooling suggests a batch window depending on SLO.
[02:52] Lena Park: That's the key tradeoff — Optimize suggests batching and KV/prefix caching to get down to low cost while still hitting latency SLOs for most traffic. For example, prefix cache will reduce token compute for repeated prompts like triage scripts.
[03:10] Maya Chen: Does prefix caching work with chat-style KV cache? We use long context sometimes — like 2k tokens.
[03:17] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we have KV cache support and partial prefix reuse. With long contexts you hit memory limits so we recommend a caching policy plus a compatible quant profile.
[03:29] Dr. Aisha: We're also obligated to SOC 2 type stuff, and need audit logs and key management.
[03:36] Lena Park: Redwood Private offers a private control plane and you can integrate your KMS / HSM. Audit logs, RBAC and SAML/SSO are supported. For SOC 2 we have compliance docs — I'll share the pack.
[03:50] Tom Ellis: For private, do you run the control plane in our VPC or is it a managed plane?
[03:55] Marco Ruiz: For Private we can do customer-managed control plane in your VPC or an on-prem package. The runtime itself runs in your environment so PHI never leaves. There are some ops considerations — networking, ingress egress, and version pinning.
[04:12] Lena Park: Back to the catalog — we also surface recommended models by workload. For short conversational triage we often recommend a 7B-ish open model in q4-fast or a tuned 13B in q4-precise if you need better instruction-following.
[04:28] Maya Chen: Any guidance on hallucination / quality regressions with lower-bit quant?
[04:32] Marco Ruiz: Yes, that's why we run evals tied to your prompt sets. Optimize can run quality regression checks against a baseline prompt set and alert if accuracy drops beyond a threshold.
[04:45] Dr. Aisha: Can you run those evals on our own data?
[04:48] Marco Ruiz: Yep, with Private we can run evals inside your environment — repo of prompts and reference outputs stay inside your network.
[04:55] [05:00] Lena Park: I'm going to switch to a benchmark slide with a compatibility matrix. This is where we map models to hardware and note support caveats like fused kernels, attention shapes, and memory peaks.
[05:18] Marco Ruiz: Example row: Llama-2-13B (open weights) — fp16: supported and yields p50 ~60ms single-stream on A100-40GB; q4-fast: supported with custom kernels, memory drops ~40% and latency ~x0.7 but quality delta is small on triage prompts. For CPU-only it's not recommended for production due to high latency.
[05:42] Tom Ellis: How about MPS/Apple silicon? We have some edge devices but not for PHI.
[05:47] Marco Ruiz: MPS is supported for smaller models but not at the same performance level. For mission critical PHI we recommend dedicated GPUs.
[05:58] Maya Chen: Any gotchas for Kubernetes deployments? We run K8s with mixed instance types.
[06:03] Marco Ruiz: The compatibility matrix has columns for K8s, on-prem GPU drivers, cuda/rocm versions. We recommend a node group per GPU class and ensure CUDA 12+ for our compiled kernels. Also watch for nvidia-driver versions and BI (binary) mismatches — we capture that in the matrix.
[06:23] Dr. Aisha: Do you support ROCm for AMD GPUs?
[06:26] Marco Ruiz: We have experimental ROCm support for some models; performance varies. For a pilot we can validate on your hardware.
[06:33] [06:45] Lena Park: Let's demo the Console quickly — model catalog UI shows measured throughput, latency windows, and quant recommendation buttons. You can filter by sequence length, target latency, and hardware.
[06:59] Lena Park: (screen share) Here we pick a triage workload, set p95 < 150ms, choose target cost, and the console suggests two candidate models and quant profiles with expected token cost and achieved latency.
[07:20] Maya Chen: The console's suggestion looks similar to what we need. Can we export the compatibility matrix?
[07:24] Lena Park: Yes CSV export. I'll include that in the artifacts.
[07:30] Tom Ellis: A quick question on routing — if you have both hosted and private, can requests automatically route based on data sensitivity?
[07:36] Marco Ruiz: Yes, smart routing policies can route by tag: e.g., PHI -> Private, non-PHI -> Hosted. We also support fallbacks to a cheaper model if capacity is constrained.
[07:50] Dr. Aisha: What's the typical fallback behavior? If private hits a high queue, do you fail over to hosted?
[07:55] Marco Ruiz: Fallback policies are configurable. Many customers prefer a degraded local model variant rather than sending PHI offsite — but you can choose.
[08:05] [08:15] Lena Park: Now the benchmark spreadsheet — the raw numbers. For the 7B candidate we saw tokens/sec ~1800 at batch size 8 on A100, p95 ~110ms. For the 13B tuned model tokens/sec ~900 batch size 4, p95 ~160ms. These are ballpark; we'll send the CSV.
[08:38] Maya Chen: Do you surface per-token cost estimates for hosted vs dedicated?
[08:41] Lena Park: Yep, Console shows estimated cost per 1k tokens for hosted; for Dedicated we provide a unit economics calc based on committed capacity and expected utilization. Optimize has heuristics for batching/caching to reduce effective cost.
[08:59] Tom Ellis: On dedicated, how do you handle autoscaling and burst capacity? We have usage spikes at appointment booking times.
[09:07] Marco Ruiz: Dedicated supports configured autoscaling policies with a buffer and burst capacity option; SLA depends on commitment tier. Burst capacity is typically subject to pre-defined limits but useful for short bursts.
[09:18] Dr. Aisha: Security again — can you ingest and store logs in our logging cluster? We need audit trail build into our SIEM.
[09:25] Lena Park: Yes, audit logs can be exported to your SIEM, and we support streaming to S3 with encryption and you can use your KMS.
[09:34] [09:45] Maya Chen: For the compatibility matrix you mentioned attention kernel changes — do you recompile kernels per customer?
[09:50] Marco Ruiz: We don't recompile per customer. We ship pre-built kernels chosen by our kernel selector at runtime; on Private you can pin kernel versions. If a customer has a custom architecture we do a validation run and can provide tuned builds as an engagement.
[10:08] Tom Ellis: What's the onboarding time for Private? Weeks or months?
[10:12] Lena Park: For a standard VPC deployment it's usually 4-6 weeks; full on-prem with custom hardware validation can be 8-12 weeks. For pilots we often do a hybrid: private control plane in VPC with runtime in your cluster, which shortens timeline.
[10:28] Dr. Aisha: Cost question: if we move some calls to q4-fast, how much quality risk are we taking for triage?
[10:34] Marco Ruiz: For triage prompts quality delta tends to be small across q4-fast vs fp16 for many open models — but we always recommend running your prompts in a small evaluation harness. That's what Optimize does: run the prompt set and show per-prompt deltas.
[10:49] [11:00] Lena Park: We also provide a compatibility matrix example in the pack: columns include model, recommended quant profile, supported hardware, required driver, expected p95 (single-stream), tokens/sec at sample batch sizes, known caveats.
[11:18] Maya Chen: Can you show an example of a compatibility row for a 13B tuned model?
[11:22] Marco Ruiz: Sure: Model: Community-13B-v1; Quant: q4-precise recommended; HW: A100-80GB or A100-40GB with >40GB usable memory; Driver: CUDA 12.1, Nvidia driver 535+; p95 single-stream: ~150-170ms; Notes: kernel fusion needed for optimal perf, check for custom tokenizers.
[11:46] Tom Ellis: Tokenizer issues — we use a modified tokenizer for clinical terms. Any pitfalls?
[11:52] Marco Ruiz: Tokenizer mismatches are real — if you change tokenization the token counts change and can affect cost and perf. We recommend shipping your tokenizer and doing a tokenization dry-run during pilot.
[12:04] [12:15] Dr. Aisha: Let's talk SLA and pilot sizing. We want a pilot to validate p95 < 150ms for triage with 95% of traffic.
[12:23] Lena Park: Sounds reasonable. For that we'd recommend a dedicated 2-GPU pool for the pilot with autoscale headroom and a 90-day trial. We'll draft an SLA and price.
[12:34] Maya Chen: For pilot metrics, what will you instrument? We need cost, latency histogram, per-route token breakdown, and quality regressions.
[12:42] Marco Ruiz: We'll provide per-route dashboards, token-level cost, p50/p95/p99 latencies, trace hooks, and quality eval hooks tied to prompts. All visible in Console and exportable.
[12:57] [13:15] Lena Park: Quick Q from me — are there any blockers on your side for starting a pilot?
[13:21] Tom Ellis: Main blockers: procurement sign-off on pilot T&Cs, and a short hardware validation for our on-prem nodes (driver compat). Also we need to confirm encryption key arrangements.
[13:32] Dr. Aisha: Legal will want details on data flow and proof PHI doesn't leave for private workloads.
[13:38] Lena Park: We'll include a data flow diagram and a short security brief. I'll have AE legal liaison follow up.
[13:46] [14:00] Marco Ruiz: One more technical note: if you plan to use long contexts (2k tokens), be aware of KV-cache memory growth. Quant profiles reduce memory but test for worst-case conversation length.
[14:16] Maya Chen: For long contexts do you support sliding window or selective truncation?
[14:20] Marco Ruiz: Yes, you can configure context management policies in the runtime: windowing, summary compression, or selective retention.
[14:32] Tom Ellis: Any example customers in healthcare?
[14:36] Lena Park: We have a few names we can share in the pack; many run in Private due to compliance.
[14:44] [15:00] Dr. Aisha: On cost, we need a clear compare: hosted per-token vs dedicated amortized cost.
[15:06] Lena Park: We'll send a unit economics model with the deck. It shows break-even utilization for dedicated at ~35-45% depending on model and quant.
[15:20] Maya Chen: Last technical: are there any models you strongly recommend avoiding for PHI?
[15:25] Marco Ruiz: Not necessarily avoiding, but older community models with small vocabularies sometimes mis-handle clinical terms — we recommend validated models and a small tuning step.
[15:36] [15:50] Lena Park: Ok time check, ~30 minutes left — want to open for deeper questions or we can go into a short technical appendix.
[15:58] Tom Ellis: Let's go a bit deeper on compatibility matrix and kernels.
[16:02] Marco Ruiz: Cool — in the appendix we show kernel-level notes: fused attention is important for long sequences; some kernels are memory-bandwidth bound and others are compute-bound. For A100 we pick the optimal kernel at runtime based on sequence length heuristics.
[16:24] Maya Chen: For our use case many messages are 64-256 tokens — what's the sweet spot?
[16:29] Marco Ruiz: 64-256 is common; batching helps but careful about p99. We typically configure a small batch window (20-50ms) for triage to avoid p99 spikes.
[16:43] Dr. Aisha: Anything else we should run during pilot?
[16:47] Marco Ruiz: A small eval set (100-200 prompts) of clinical examples, a perf harness for peak-hour simulation, and a tokenizer dry-run.
[16:58] [17:15] Lena Park: Final recap — Lena to send deck, benchmark CSV, compatibility matrix; Marco to prep infra checklist and quant notes; Tom to send traffic profile and legal to review. We'll schedule deep-dive next week.
[17:33] Tom Ellis: Sounds good, thanks.
[17:38] Dr. Aisha: Thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[17:42] Lena Park: Thank you all. We'll follow up by Friday with artifacts and a proposed pilot scope.
[17:50] Maya Chen: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
